title: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
summary: Builds four RL environments (traffic control, COVID response, Atari Riverraid, glucose monitoring) with nine misspecified proxy rewards, taxonomized as misweighting, ontological or scope misspecification, and trains agents of varying optimization power (model size, training steps, action resolution, observation fidelity). More capable agents often get higher proxy and lower true reward; five of nine proxies lead to 'misalignment' (low true reward) and four show phase transitions where behavior shifts qualitatively. Reward hacking occurs even when proxy and true rewards are positively correlated. Proposes Polynomaly, an anomaly-detection benchmark for aberrant policies, with distance-based baselines that each have at least one subtask with AUROC under 60%.
setting: PPO (traffic, COVID), SAC (glucose), IMPALA/torchbeast (Atari); Flow/SUMO traffic simulator, SEIR COVID model, FDA-approved glucose simulator; parameter counts varied by two to four orders of magnitude.

quotes.quote: Reward misspecifications occur because real-world tasks have numerous, often conflicting desiderata. In practice, reward designers resort to optimizing a proxy reward that is either more readily measured or more easily optimized than the true reward.
In general, misweighting occurs when the proxy and true reward capture the same desiderata, but differ on their relative importance.
In general, ontological misspecification occurs when the proxy and true reward use different desiderata to capture the same concept.
In general, scope misspecification occurs when the proxy measures desiderata over a restricted domain (e.g. time, space).

key_numbers.claim: Counts of misalignment and phase transitions across nine proxies
key_numbers.quote: We observe 5 instances of misalignment and 4 instances of phase transitions.
Each detector has at least one subtask with AUROC under 60%, indicating poor performance.

limitations_stated: Model size is only one proxy for capability (checked with training steps, action resolution, observation fidelity); baseline detectors are weak; detectors would be optimized against and need adversarial robustness; trend extrapolation cannot catch phase transitions.
open_questions: How to prevent, not just detect, phase transitions; how to mitigate misalignment when the true reward is not observed.
sense_of_alignment: Alignment as an RL policy scoring well on the designer's true reward rather than a misspecified proxy; the paper labels a proxy as leading to 'misalignment (i.e. to a policy with low true reward)'.
